units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Wall Street crash of 1929] "On October 24, \"Black Thursday\", the market lost 11% of its value at the opening bell."; "It is most associated with October 24, 1929, known as \"Black Thursday\""
units.note: Both quotes are verbatim. 'Soon after trading opened' is a fair and more cautious reading of 'at the opening bell'. The 11% intraday fall built up over the morning. The year is given in frame 1 ('in 1929'). The spoken line says the same thing as the caption, with the date read out.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Wall Street crash of 1929] "The Dow Jones Industrial Average recovered, closing down only 6.38 points (2.09%) for the day."
units.note: The key is right (2.09%). 'About 11 percent' is the intraday fall, not the close, so it is a good wrong choice. 'About 25 percent' is wrong. The reveal (index 3, 'The Dow closed down only about 2 percent') comes after frame 2's 11% figure, which supports the distractor rather than giving the key away. Frame 0, shown behind the question, is the crowd photo, with no number. The title 'The crash that paused' (on hub cards and in the aria-label) hints that the fall stopped, but not that it recovered, so 11% stays a plausible choice.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Ocelot] "The ocelot is efficient at climbing, leaping and swimming."; "The name \"ocelot\" comes from the Nahuatl word ōcēlōtl (pronounced [oːˈseːloːt͡ɬ]), which generally refers to the jaguar, rather than the ocelot. Another possible origin for the name is the Latin ocellatus"
units.note: 'May come from' correctly hedges the source's alternative Latin etymology. The voice now keeps the final 'tl' ('oh-SAY-lohtl'), with stress on the second syllable as the IPA shows. 'Nah-wah-tul' is a fair English respelling. The image m5 (an ocelot on a branch at night) suits 'climbs'. Nit, no fix needed: the source says the word 'refers' (present tense) to the jaguar, and Nahuatl is still spoken, so 'means' would be slightly more exact than 'meant'.
